opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think inference cost is one of the biggest practical barriers right now, and people often underestimate it. When you think about a gamer, the economics are really unforgiving. Someone buys a game for, say, sixty or seventy dollars, and they might play it for hundreds of hours. If you put a large frontier model behind every NPC or every companion agent, and it's thinking continuously, perceiving the screen, planning, talking back, the cloud bill per player can very quickly exceed what the player paid for the game. That just doesn't work as a business.

And it's not only dollars, it's latency. Games run at sixty frames per second. An agent that takes two or three seconds to respond feels broken in a fast-paced game. So you have this double constraint: it has to be cheap and it has to be fast.

So I think a few things will happen. First, a lot of the intelligence has to move on-device. Gamers already have very capable GPUs sitting in their machines, and that's essentially free compute from the developer's perspective. So distilling big models into small, specialized ones that can run locally alongside the game engine is going to be really important. Second, you'll see hierarchical systems: a small, fast model handles the moment-to-moment reflexes and dialogue, and only occasionally you call a bigger model in the cloud for higher-level reasoning or long-term planning. It's a bit like System 1 and System 2.

Third, I'm optimistic because the cost curve is dropping incredibly fast. The price per token for a given level of capability has been falling by roughly an order of magnitude every year or so. Things that are prohibitively expensive today will be cheap in two or three years. So I'd say inference cost shapes how we design these agents today, but I don't think it's a fundamental blocker. It's more of a timing question. The developers who start building the experiences now, assuming compute will get cheaper, will be in a great position when the economics catch up.

r001.rationale: The response says continuous frontier-model cloud inference could cost more per player than the game earns, and proposes running smaller models locally on gamers’ GPUs. This communicates the need for affordable cloud inference or local device inference.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is actually the thing I think about most, because people underestimate how brutal the gaming use case is on economics. Think about the numbers. A big game can have millions of concurrent players, and each session lasts hours. If you want an agent that's genuinely a companion or a teammate, something that sees the screen, reasons about what's happening, and acts at the frame rate the game demands, you're running inference continuously, not in little bursts like a chatbot. So the cost per user-hour matters way more than cost per query, and a few cents an hour multiplied across a player base adds up to a budget nobody in gaming has, because gaming margins are thin to begin with.

So the constraint shapes the architecture. You can't put a frontier model in the loop for every frame. What you end up with is a hierarchy. A tiny policy, maybe tens of millions of parameters, running on the local GPU or even the console, handling the fast reactive stuff: aiming, moving, dodging. Then a mid-size model doing tactical planning every few seconds. And only occasionally do you escalate to a big model in the cloud for things like dialogue or long-horizon strategy, and that call gets amortized across a lot of gameplay. Honestly, this is a lot like how we structure robot brains too, with a slow deliberate layer and a fast reflex layer.

The other thing inference cost does is push you toward distillation. You use the expensive model as a teacher offline, generate tons of trajectories, and compress that behavior into a small student that's cheap at runtime. Gamers already have a GPU sitting under their desk, which is this massive untapped compute resource. If the model fits locally, your marginal cost goes to zero and latency drops to nothing, and that's where I think the really interesting agents live.

So my take is: inference cost isn't a reason it won't happen, it's the reason the agents won't look like ChatGPT with a controller. They'll look like small, specialized, locally running models that know when to ask a bigger brain for help.

r001.rationale: The response says agents should use small models running locally on a gamer’s GPU or console, making runtime marginal cost effectively zero. This satisfies the local-inference option.

astra-6.text:
I think inference cost is one of the biggest constraints. In a game, you’re not asking an agent a question and waiting a few seconds for an answer. The agent has to keep observing, making decisions, and acting. And if you have millions of players, each interacting with multiple agents, that cost adds up very quickly.

So you probably don’t want a large model thinking through every single frame. You want a hierarchy: a larger model handles the high-level planning, and a smaller, faster model executes those plans. The high-level model might decide, “Let’s go collect resources,” while the low-level policy handles moving around and interacting with objects.

The exciting thing about games is that you can train and evaluate those smaller policies in simulation. But ultimately, the agent has to fit within the game’s latency and compute budget. Being intelligent isn’t enough—it has to be affordable to run continuously.

r001.rationale: The response says inference costs add up at scale and agents must fit the game’s compute budget, but it does not state that deployment requires very low-cost cloud inference or inference on gamers’ devices.

sol-6.1.text:
For gamers, the constraint is pretty unforgiving: you need low latency, and you need to serve a lot of people at once. If every character has to call a large model every time it decides what to do, the cost adds up very quickly—and the player is still waiting for a response.

So I think you need different levels of computation. A larger model might handle a high-level goal or an unusual situation, while a smaller model handles the frequent, moment-to-moment actions. You don’t need to rethink the entire plan every frame.

The exciting part is that games give you an environment where you can train and evaluate those smaller policies. You can spend more compute during training so that execution becomes cheaper. Ultimately, the agent has to fit within the economics of the game. A compelling demo with one player is very different from something millions of people can play every day.

r001.rationale: The response says inference must be economical at scale and suggests smaller models for frequent actions, but it does not state that inference must be low-cost in the cloud or run locally on gamers’ devices.
